text: Lakeview Facilities has its groups, one ACL, one catalog item, and one notification from Lesson 35. Three things remain before this is genuinely production-ready: form-behavior rules on the request itself, a sanity check on the platform settings that affect this department, and a disciplined way to move the whole build out of Dev.

The request needs one more rule: destination location becomes required when request type is Relocation. A UI Policy handles that on the form. But the same rule needs a server-side backstop — a Data Policy with the identical condition — because if a Relocation request ever reaches the table through an API, an import, or a script that bypasses the form, the UI Policy does nothing at all. The Data Policy still holds.

Before calling this done, check two platform settings that actually touch Lakeview. First, the instance's outbound email property — a notification can be configured perfectly and still never send if outbound email is off at the instance level. Second, whether an existing scheduled job that auto-closes stale requests actually covers the new Facilities Request table, or was only ever scoped to Incident. Confirm both in System Logs rather than assuming silence means success.

None of this should have been built directly in Production. Every piece — groups and roles, the ACL, the catalog item and its variable set, the notification, and the new UI and Data Policies — belongs inside one well-named Update Set. But user records and group membership are never captured by that set at all; they have to exist independently in each environment.

Complete the set only once everything's tested together in Dev. Move it to Test first, where someone other than you — ideally an actual coordinator — walks through submitting and fulfilling one real request. Only after that passes do you commit the same set in Production. If a problem turns up, fix it in Dev and move a corrected set through the same path — never hand-patch Production directly.

Seven checks make a setup production-ready: group mapping, real field-level ACLs instead of UI-only hiding, correct catalog routing, end-to-end tested notifications, UI Policies paired with Data Policies wherever integrity matters, confirmed properties and scheduled jobs, and one clean Update Set verified by someone else before Production. That closes this course. Next up: Flow Designer and Automation, course four of fourteen in this path.
